body:
## Module 1 in two minutes

**You're ahead on AI, on the wrong axis.** Your function adopted it faster than almost any other part of People, and almost entirely for drafting. Drafting was never the constraint. The constraints are two budgets AI can't touch: **attention**, which is finite, shared, non-renewable inside a week, and not yours; and **belief**, which is earned slowly, spent instantly, and is the one input no model can manufacture.

**Volume is now measured as an organizational risk** `[V]`. High-volume communication environments show a 30% increase in leadership-trust risk and a 24% rise in audience burnout, and 83% of the profession says overload is growing. Note the sample (communicators, not employees) which makes it a strong directional signal rather than a coefficient.

**What AI removed was the rationing mechanism.** Writing used to cost time, and that time forced somebody to decide the message was worth it. The tools removed the time and replaced the decision with nothing. So the first-order effect on this function is degradation, and because the fix is a norms problem, it belongs to you.

### The rule to carry

**Your function's product is not content. It is attention converted into belief.** AI made the raw material free and left both budgets exactly where they were. When you evaluate any new initiative, ask one question: *after this ships, who decides whether the next message is worth sending?* An initiative that makes sending automatic hasn't reduced the cost of communicating. It has removed the last person who was deciding.

**The full module adds** the diagnosis — 75% of internal comms functions are still ad hoc with AI, and the maturity split is the finding: low-maturity teams use it to draft, high-maturity teams use it to measure and target `[V]`, so the profession adopted AI where it is most dangerous and least where it would help. Plus the four-initiative exercise, the course's refusal to re-teach prompting, and the send audit that opens the attention ledger every later module writes to. Discovering that nobody in your organization can produce the number is a finding, and it scores at full credit.
